languages.name: Python

rules.types: Dynamic typing; optional annotations are not normally runtime-enforced. None is the null value; bool is an int subclass.
rules.blocks: Indentation defines suites after a colon. Use consistent spaces; newlines usually end statements.
rules.comments: # starts a line comment. Triple-quoted strings are strings and can serve as docstrings, not block-comment syntax.
rules.variables: Assignment binds names to objects. Objects may be mutable or immutable; assignment does not copy them. Scope uses local, enclosing, global and built-in names.
rules.functions: def defines functions; arguments may be positional or keyword. Default argument expressions are evaluated once when the definition runs.
rules.control_flow: if/elif/else, for over iterables, while, break and continue. and/or short-circuit and return operands, not necessarily booleans.
rules.collections: list, tuple, dict and set; slicing usually excludes the stop index. Dictionary keys and set members must be hashable.
rules.errors: raise and try/except/else/finally; with manages context-bound cleanup. Exception handling does not replace input validation.
rules.modules: import loads modules and may execute their top-level code. Packages and environments determine dependency resolution.
rules.runtime: Python interpreter; arbitrary-precision integers, floating-point approximations. CPython commonly uses reference counting plus cycle collection.

pitfalls: / is true division; // floors, including negative results.
Mutable default arguments and shallow copies can share state unexpectedly.
Do not translate Python truthiness, equality, indexing or async behavior by spelling alone.

languages.name: JavaScript

rules.types: Dynamic typing; primitive values include string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol and null. Objects have reference identity.
rules.blocks: Braces delimit blocks. Automatic semicolon insertion exists but can change meaning at line boundaries.
rules.comments: // line comments and /* block comments */; block comments do not nest.
rules.variables: let and const are block-scoped; const prevents rebinding, not object mutation. var is function-scoped.
rules.functions: Function declarations/expressions and arrows; arrows capture lexical this. Closures retain access to enclosing bindings.
rules.control_flow: if/else, switch, loops and try. for...of iterates iterable values; for...in enumerates enumerable string property keys.
rules.collections: Arrays, objects, Map and Set. Array holes differ from explicit undefined; strings expose UTF-16 code units through indexing.
rules.errors: throw and try/catch/finally. Promise rejection must be handled; async functions return promises.
rules.modules: ES import/export; CommonJS require is a host convention, not ES module syntax. Resolution depends on browser or runtime.
rules.runtime: Browser or server engine with host APIs. Number uses IEEE-754 doubles; BigInt is distinct. Event-loop tasks and microtasks affect ordering.

pitfalls: == coerces operands; === avoids most cross-type equality coercion.
Number cannot exactly represent every integer above 2^53 - 1.
DOM APIs are not general Node.js APIs; asynchronous control flow needs deliberate mapping.

languages.name: TypeScript

rules.types: Static structural type checking layered over JavaScript; unions, interfaces and generics. Nullable unions depend on strictNullChecks. any bypasses many checks; unknown requires narrowing.
rules.blocks: JavaScript braces and statement rules plus type syntax. TSX also permits JSX and has additional parsing constraints.
rules.comments: // and /* */. Compiler directives in comments can affect checking and must not be silently carried over.
rules.variables: let/const with annotations or inference. readonly is generally a compile-time constraint, not runtime freezing.
rules.functions: Typed parameters, return annotations, overload signatures and generics. Implementation still obeys JavaScript runtime semantics.
rules.control_flow: JavaScript control flow plus type narrowing through guards and discriminated unions. Narrowing is not general runtime validation.
rules.collections: Array<T>, tuples, Record, Map and Set. Types do not automatically validate JSON or external input.
rules.errors: JavaScript exceptions/promises; static checks do not prove code cannot throw. Catch-variable typing depends on settings.
rules.modules: import/export with type-only imports. tsconfig module, target and resolution settings control emitted code and lookup.
rules.runtime: Typically compiled to JavaScript; type annotations are erased. Some constructs such as enums can emit runtime code. Requires a suitable JS host.

pitfalls: Do not strip types with regex; JSX, generics, enums and module syntax require a real compiler.
strictNullChecks and other tsconfig settings change what the checker accepts.
A successful type check does not validate untrusted network data.

languages.name: Java

rules.types: Static nominal typing; primitives differ from reference types. Generics usually use reference types and erase most type arguments at runtime.
rules.blocks: Braces form blocks; statements normally end with semicolons. Source organization follows classes and packages.
rules.comments: //, /* */ and documentation comments /** */.
rules.variables: Explicit types or local var inference; final prevents reassignment, not necessarily mutation of the referenced object.
rules.functions: Methods belong to classes/interfaces; static methods do not require an instance. Arguments are passed by value, including reference values.
rules.control_flow: if, switch, for, enhanced for, while and do/while; conditions require boolean expressions.
rules.collections: Fixed-length arrays and collection interfaces such as List, Set and Map. Equality and hashing contracts matter.
rules.errors: try/catch/finally, throw/throws and try-with-resources. Checked exceptions impose declaration/handling requirements.
rules.modules: package/import and optional Java platform modules. Imports name types; build tools resolve artifacts separately.
rules.runtime: Usually compiled to JVM bytecode with garbage collection. Fixed-width integer overflow wraps; integer division truncates toward zero.

pitfalls: == compares reference identity for objects; equals is used for value contracts.
Null references, boxing and checked exceptions need explicit porting decisions.
String indexing is based on UTF-16 code units, not user-visible characters.

languages.name: C

rules.types: Static types; integer widths and signedness can depend on implementation. Pointers refer to objects or functions; arrays are not pointers.
rules.blocks: Braces form compound statements; semicolons terminate most statements. Preprocessor directives are handled before compilation.
rules.comments: /* */ and, since C99, //; block comments do not nest.
rules.variables: Declarations have types, storage duration and scope. Automatic locals are not implicitly initialized.
rules.functions: Typed function declarations/prototypes; arguments are passed by value. Pointer parameters can expose caller-owned data.
rules.control_flow: if, switch, for, while, do/while and goto. Zero is false; nonzero is true.
rules.collections: Arrays and structs; dynamic collections require libraries or explicit allocation. Ordinary strings use a null terminator.
rules.errors: No language exceptions; use return codes and API-specific errno contracts. Release allocated resources on every path.
rules.modules: Headers, #include, translation units and linker symbols; macro expansion is not a language-aware module import.
rules.runtime: Normally native machine code. Explicit allocation/free and object-lifetime rules; undefined behavior is not a portable outcome.

pitfalls: Signed overflow, out-of-bounds access and use-after-free can be undefined behavior.
Array length and ownership do not travel with a bare pointer.
.h is ambiguous between C and C++; toolchain and include context decide.

languages.name: C++

rules.types: Static typing with classes, templates, references and pointers. auto infers types; value category affects overload resolution and moves.
rules.blocks: Braces and semicolon-terminated statements; namespaces organize names. Preprocessor and templates are distinct mechanisms.
rules.comments: // and /* */; block comments do not nest.
rules.variables: Initialization forms differ; object lifetime and const qualification matter. RAII binds resource cleanup to object lifetime.
rules.functions: Free/member functions, overloads, templates and lambdas. Parameters can pass values or references; captures affect lifetime.
rules.control_flow: if, switch, loops and range-for. Destructors run during normal scope exit and exception unwinding for constructed automatic objects.
rules.collections: std::vector, array, map, unordered_map and string. Iterator invalidation depends on container and operation.
rules.errors: Exceptions, error codes and vocabulary types such as optional. noexcept is a contract with termination consequences if violated.
rules.modules: C++17 commonly uses headers, translation units, namespaces and linking; language modules require a later baseline.
rules.runtime: Usually native code with deterministic destruction. Prefer standard containers and smart pointers; undefined behavior still exists.

pitfalls: Moves, copies, reference lifetimes and ownership cannot be translated as mere assignment syntax.
Signed overflow and dangling references are not guaranteed runtime errors.
Compiler ABI, templates and native dependencies can prevent a mechanical port.

languages.name: C#

rules.types: Static typing with value/reference types, interfaces and generics. Nullable value types differ from nullable-reference annotations.
rules.blocks: Braces form blocks; semicolons end most statements. File-scoped namespaces and top-level statements have placement rules.
rules.comments: //, /* */ and /// XML documentation comments.
rules.variables: Explicit types or var inference. const values and readonly fields have different initialization and mutation contracts.
rules.functions: Methods, local functions, lambdas and delegates. ref/out/in affect parameter passing; async methods commonly return Task.
rules.control_flow: if, switch/patterns, foreach, for, while, break and continue; await composes asynchronous operations.
rules.collections: Arrays, List<T>, Dictionary<TKey,TValue>, spans and IEnumerable<T>; LINQ queries can be deferred.
rules.errors: throw and try/catch/finally. using/await using provide deterministic cleanup for disposable resources.
rules.modules: Namespaces and using declarations organize names; assemblies/projects and package references define build dependencies.
rules.runtime: Usually managed .NET execution with garbage collection. Integer overflow behavior depends on checked context and operation.

pitfalls: Value-type copies differ from reference-type aliases.
Nullable annotations do not enforce every runtime non-null guarantee.
Task scheduling, UI thread affinity and deferred LINQ need behavior tests.

languages.name: Go

rules.types: Static typing with inference, structs, interfaces and type parameters. Interfaces are implemented implicitly; nil has context-dependent typed forms.
rules.blocks: Braces are required for control blocks; semicolons are often inserted automatically. Opening-brace placement matters.
rules.comments: // and /* */; special build directives have additional placement and formatting rules.
rules.variables: var declarations or local := short declarations; constants have distinct typing rules. Exported identifiers start with an uppercase letter.
rules.functions: func declarations, methods with receivers, closures and multiple return values. Arguments are passed by value.
rules.control_flow: if, for, switch and select; there is no separate while keyword. defer schedules calls for function exit.
rules.collections: Arrays have fixed length in their type; slices share backing arrays. Maps are reference-like and have unspecified iteration order.
rules.errors: Ordinary failures conventionally return error values. panic/recover are not a replacement for routine error handling.
rules.modules: package/import plus go.mod modules; import cycles are rejected. Module path and package name are distinct.
rules.runtime: Compiled code with garbage collection; goroutines and channels support concurrency. Data-race freedom remains the program's responsibility.

pitfalls: Copying a slice header does not copy its backing storage.
A non-nil interface can hold a nil pointer.
Range-loop variable behavior differs across language versions; check the module's go directive.

languages.name: Rust

rules.types: Static typing with inference, traits, enums and generics. Ownership, borrowing and lifetimes constrain access to values.
rules.blocks: Braced blocks are expressions. A trailing semicolon discards an expression's value; a final expression can become the block result.
rules.comments: //, nested /* */ and documentation comments /// or //!.
rules.variables: let bindings are immutable by default; mut permits mutation. Binding moves or copies depend on the value's type.
rules.functions: fn with typed parameters and optional -> return type; closures capture by borrow or move depending on use and declaration.
rules.control_flow: if, match, loop, while and for. match is exhaustive; patterns can bind or destructure values.
rules.collections: Arrays, Vec<T>, slices, HashMap and String. String is UTF-8; integer indexing of String is not supported.
rules.errors: Result<T,E> and Option<T>, with ? for compatible early propagation. panic is separate from ordinary recoverable errors.
rules.modules: mod/use, visibility and crates; Cargo manages packages and dependencies. Macro expansion is not plain text substitution.
rules.runtime: Usually native code without a tracing garbage collector; ownership drives destruction. unsafe permits operations requiring extra invariants.

pitfalls: Do not erase borrowing/lifetime constraints when mapping to a garbage-collected language.
Integer overflow behavior can depend on build checks; explicit checked/wrapping APIs make intent clearer.
A string byte offset need not be a Unicode character boundary.

languages.name: Swift

rules.types: Static typing with inference, protocols, generics and optionals. Structs/enums have value semantics; classes have reference semantics.
rules.blocks: Braces delimit scopes; semicolons are usually optional at line ends.
rules.comments: // and nestable /* */; documentation comments have tooling conventions.
rules.variables: let creates constants and var variables. A constant class reference does not necessarily freeze the instance.
rules.functions: func declarations, argument labels, closures and inout parameters. async/await supports concurrency.
rules.control_flow: if, guard, switch, for-in, while and repeat-while. switch is exhaustive; optional binding unwraps conditionally.
rules.collections: Array, Set and Dictionary with value semantics, often copy-on-write implementations. String indexes are not integer offsets.
rules.errors: throw/throws, do/catch and try variants; defer schedules scope-exit cleanup. Force unwraps can trap.
rules.modules: import loads module interfaces; packages and platform frameworks provide dependencies.
rules.runtime: Compiled code with automatic reference counting for class instances. Standard arithmetic can trap on overflow; wrapping operators are explicit.

pitfalls: Optionals are not interchangeable with unchecked null references.
ARC cycles, weak references and value/reference distinctions affect behavior.
UIKit/AppKit and Apple-specific frameworks do not become portable simply by translating syntax.

languages.name: Kotlin

rules.types: Static typing with inference, nullable types, classes and generics. Platform types from Java weaken normal null-safety guarantees.
rules.blocks: Braces form blocks; semicolons are generally optional. Some control constructs are expressions.
rules.comments: //, nested /* */ and KDoc comments /** */.
rules.variables: val prevents rebinding; var allows it. A val can reference mutable state. Properties may have custom accessors.
rules.functions: fun, extension functions, lambdas and named/default arguments. suspend marks functions usable in coroutine contexts.
rules.control_flow: if, when, for-in and while; smart casts require suitable stability guarantees. Ranges can be inclusive.
rules.collections: Read-only List/Set/Map interfaces differ from MutableList/MutableSet/MutableMap, but do not universally guarantee immutable storage.
rules.errors: try/catch/finally and throw; exceptions are unchecked at the language level. Resource management helpers depend on target libraries.
rules.modules: package/import, source sets and build-tool dependencies; JVM, JS and Native targets expose different APIs.
rules.runtime: Execution model depends on target. Kotlin/JVM runs on the JVM; multiplatform source still needs compatible libraries.

pitfalls: == calls structural equality; === checks referential identity.
!! can throw; null-safety is not proof that platform interop cannot fail.
Coroutines are not mechanically interchangeable with threads or promises.

languages.name: PHP

rules.types: Dynamic typing with optional declarations, unions and nullable types. Coercion and strict_types affect scalar-call behavior.
rules.blocks: Braces and semicolons; alternative template syntax exists. PHP segments typically begin with <?php.
rules.comments: //, # and /* */; block comments do not nest.
rules.variables: $-prefixed names; scope and reference bindings with & require care. Assignment and object-handle behavior differ by value kind.
rules.functions: function declarations and closures; arrow functions capture outer variables by value. Arguments can be named or positional.
rules.control_flow: if/elseif/else, switch, match and loops. foreach supports array/object iteration; by-reference iteration requires special care.
rules.collections: array is an ordered map with integer/string keys and coercion rules; it is not solely a numeric vector.
rules.errors: Throwable includes Error and Exception; use try/catch/finally. Warnings and diagnostics are not always thrown exceptions.
rules.modules: Namespaces, include/require and autoloading. Composer package management is separate from language syntax.
rules.runtime: PHP runtime, commonly CLI or request-based server execution. Web output, superglobals and host configuration affect behavior.

languages.example:
<?php
function total(array $values): int {
    return array_sum($values);
}
echo total([1, 2, 3]), PHP_EOL;
pitfalls: == coercion differs from === and has changed across PHP versions.
Array key coercion and empty/isset semantics need explicit tests.
Translation must preserve escaping, authentication and database parameterization, not just web output.

languages.name: Ruby

rules.types: Dynamic typing; values are objects. nil and false are falsey; zero and empty strings are truthy.
rules.blocks: Many constructs end with end. Blocks passed to methods use do/end or braces, with precedence differences.
rules.comments: # line comments; =begin/=end have line-position requirements. Documentation tooling generally uses line comments.
rules.variables: Local names, @instance, @@class and $global variables have distinct scopes; uppercase-leading names denote constants.
rules.functions: def defines methods; blocks, Proc and lambda have different return/argument behavior. Methods return their last expression by default.
rules.control_flow: if/unless, case, while/until and iterator methods; each yields values to a block. Modifier conditionals are supported.
rules.collections: Array, Hash and ranges; inclusive .. ranges differ from exclusive-end ... ranges. Symbols are distinct from strings.
rules.errors: raise and begin/rescue/ensure; rescue without a class normally catches StandardError descendants, not every Exception.
rules.modules: require/load files; modules group names and can be mixed into classes. Gems and Bundler manage dependencies.
rules.runtime: Ruby interpreter/implementation with garbage collection; monkey patching and metaprogramming can change runtime method lookup.

languages.example:
def total(values)
  values.sum
end
puts total([1, 2, 3])
pitfalls: Zero and empty collections are truthy, unlike some other languages.
Blocks, lambdas and procs do not have identical return semantics.
Dynamic method generation and framework conventions can hide behavior from a syntax-only port.

languages.name: R

rules.types: Dynamic, vector-oriented types; NA, NaN, NULL and Inf have different meanings. Factors encode categorical values, not plain strings.
rules.blocks: Braces group expressions; newlines or semicolons separate complete statements.
rules.comments: # line comments. Strings are data, not a general multiline comment mechanism.
rules.variables: <- commonly binds names; = is also used in suitable contexts. Lexical scope and environments govern name lookup.
rules.functions: function defines closures; arguments are usually lazy promises. A function normally returns its final evaluated expression.
rules.control_flow: if expects a single non-missing logical condition; for, while and repeat. Vectorized operations differ from scalar control flow.
rules.collections: Atomic vectors, lists, matrices and data frames. Indexing is usually one-based; [ and [[ have distinct subsetting semantics.
rules.errors: stop, warning, tryCatch and condition handlers; on.exit can register cleanup within functions.
rules.modules: Packages and namespaces; library attaches a package, while pkg::name retrieves an exported member.
rules.runtime: R interpreter with garbage collection and native extensions. Vector recycling and missing-value propagation are central semantics.

pitfalls: NA comparisons propagate missingness; use is.na instead of equality with NA.
Vector recycling, one-based indexing and column coercion need explicit mapping.
Package data structures may have class-specific dispatch and evaluation rules.

languages.name: Bash
languages.baseline: Bash 4 core; not generic POSIX sh

rules.types: Shell variables primarily hold strings; arithmetic contexts interpret integers. Arrays are a Bash feature, not universally available in POSIX sh.
rules.blocks: Keyword pairs such as if/fi and do/done; grouping with braces or parentheses has syntax and environment differences.
rules.comments: An unquoted # starts a comment when it begins a shell word in the relevant parsing context.
rules.variables: name=value assigns without spaces. Quote expansions such as "$name" to avoid unintended word splitting and globbing.
rules.functions: name() { commands; }; positional parameters use $1 etc. Local variables require local inside a function.
rules.control_flow: if/while test command exit status; zero means success. [[ ... ]] differs from [ ... ]; && and || compose commands.
rules.collections: Indexed and associative arrays; quote "${items[@]}" to preserve individual elements. Pipelines usually exchange bytes, not typed objects.
rules.errors: Exit status, explicit checks and trap. set -e has context-sensitive exceptions and is not general exception handling.
rules.modules: source or . executes a file in the current shell; external commands are resolved through PATH and environment.
rules.runtime: Bash plus operating-system utilities. Command substitution, redirection and expansion can execute programs or affect files.

languages.example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
values=(1 2 3)
sum=0
for value in "${values[@]}"; do
  sum=$((sum + value))
done
printf '%s\n' "$sum"
pitfalls: A .sh extension does not prove Bash; the shebang, launch command and shell determine the dialect.
Quoting and expansion order are security-critical; never translate by concatenating untrusted shell strings.
External utilities, exit codes and pipeline subshell behavior vary across platforms.

languages.name: PowerShell

rules.types: Dynamic object-oriented shell with .NET types, optional constraints and automatic conversions. $null has special comparison/enumeration behavior.
rules.blocks: Braces delimit script blocks; newlines or semicolons separate statements. Expression mode and argument mode parse differently.
rules.comments: # line comments and <# block comments #>; help comments have recognized conventions.
rules.variables: $name assignment; scope prefixes and environment providers change lookup. Single-quoted strings are literal; double-quoted strings expand.
rules.functions: function with param blocks; pipeline output includes uncaptured success-stream values, not just explicit return expressions.
rules.control_flow: if, switch, foreach, for, while and pipelines. foreach statement and ForEach-Object command have different execution contexts.
rules.collections: Arrays, hashtables and .NET collections. Pipelines normally carry objects; native programs add text/argument conversion boundaries.
rules.errors: Terminating and non-terminating errors differ; try/catch handles terminating errors. -ErrorAction Stop can promote many command errors.
rules.modules: Import-Module, module manifests and dot-sourcing. Loading scripts/modules can execute code; a .psd1 file is not necessarily an ordinary script.
rules.runtime: PowerShell host and .NET; platform-specific cmdlets may not exist on Linux. Native argument passing varies by host/version.

pitfalls: Unintended success-stream output can change a function's effective return value.
Exit codes from native tools and PowerShell errors require different checks.
Windows-only modules and 5.1 behavior are not guaranteed on cross-platform PowerShell 7.

languages.name: SQL
languages.baseline: Common relational SQL subset; dialect must be chosen

rules.types: Column/expression types and coercion rules depend on the database. NULL introduces unknown into three-valued predicate logic.
rules.blocks: Statements commonly end in semicolons. Procedural blocks are dialect extensions, not a universal SQL scripting syntax.
rules.comments: -- line comments and commonly /* */; nesting and whitespace requirements vary by dialect.
rules.variables: Parameters, local variables and identifier quoting are driver/dialect-specific. Bind data values rather than interpolating user text.
rules.functions: Scalar, aggregate and window functions exist; user-defined function syntax and availability differ by engine.
rules.control_flow: SELECT/FROM/WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING/ORDER BY describe queries; CASE selects expressions. Procedural loops are not universal.
rules.collections: Tables and result sets; duplicates remain unless removed. Row order is not guaranteed without a suitable ORDER BY.
rules.errors: Engine/driver errors, transactions and constraints determine failure handling. Atomicity and rollback behavior depend on engine and operation.
rules.modules: Schemas, views and migration files organize database logic; connection drivers and permissions are outside SQL text alone.
rules.runtime: Database engine/query planner. Collation, timezone, isolation and schema affect results even when query text is unchanged.

languages.example:
-- Assumes a numbers table with a numeric value column.
SELECT SUM(value) AS total
FROM numbers
WHERE value IS NOT NULL;
pitfalls: Use IS NULL, not = NULL, for null checks.
SQL dialect conversion requires a chosen source and target engine plus schema context.
A SELECT can still be costly or invoke functions; this library never connects to a database or runs it.

languages.name: Dart
languages.baseline: Dart 2.17 core with sound null safety

rules.types: Static typing with inference and sound null safety; dynamic opts out of many static checks. T? is nullable.
rules.blocks: Braces group blocks; most statements end in semicolons.
rules.comments: //, nestable /* */ and documentation comments ///.
rules.variables: var infers a type; final assigns once; const denotes compile-time constants. late postpones initialization checks.
rules.functions: Typed functions, closures and => expressions; named parameters use braces and can be required. async functions return Future values.
rules.control_flow: if, switch, loops and for-in; await and await-for consume asynchronous results/streams in appropriate contexts.
rules.collections: List, Set and Map with collection-if/collection-for and spread syntax. String indexing exposes UTF-16 units.
rules.errors: throw, try/on/catch/finally; Future errors need asynchronous handling. Assertions are not a substitute for production validation.
rules.modules: import/export and libraries; pubspec.yaml declares package dependencies. Flutter adds a framework, not a separate language.
rules.runtime: Dart VM/native or JavaScript target; isolates have separate memory and communicate by messages. Platform libraries differ by target.

pitfalls: Native and JavaScript targets can differ in integer precision and available APIs.
Isolates are not shared-memory threads.
Porting Dart does not automatically port Flutter widgets, assets or platform plugins.

languages.name: Lua

rules.types: Dynamic typing; nil, boolean, number, string, function, userdata, thread and table. Only nil and false are falsey.
rules.blocks: Keyword blocks end with end; repeat ends with until. Semicolons are usually optional.
rules.comments: -- line comments and long-bracket comments such as --[[ ... ]]; matching equals signs allow different long-bracket delimiters.
rules.variables: local limits scope; otherwise names usually resolve through the environment. Assignment can bind several names at once.
rules.functions: function definitions, closures and multiple returns. Colon method syntax supplies an implicit self argument.
rules.control_flow: if/elseif/else, while, repeat/until, numeric/generic for and break; and/or short-circuit and return operands.
rules.collections: Tables implement arrays, maps and objects. Sequence conventions start at 1; holes make length and ipairs behavior important.
rules.errors: error raises; pcall/xpcall provide protected calls. Coroutine suspension and errors have host-sensitive integration.
rules.modules: require uses package loaders; embedding hosts may replace or remove standard libraries and loading behavior.
rules.runtime: Lua VM, often embedded in another application, with garbage collection. Lua 5.4 integers/floats and APIs differ from older Lua/LuaJIT.

languages.example:
local function total(values)
  local sum = 0
  for _, value in ipairs(values) do sum = sum + value end
  return sum
end
print(total({1, 2, 3}))
pitfalls: Zero is truthy; nil removes table entries.
One-based sequence conventions and holes do not map directly to zero-based arrays.
Game-engine APIs, LuaJIT and sandboxed hosts may differ from standard Lua 5.4.

languages.name: HTML
languages.baseline: HTML core markup; browser behavior matters

rules.types: Markup describes document structure, not a general-purpose variable/type system. Elements and attributes have defined semantics.
rules.blocks: Start/end tags form elements; void elements such as img have no end tag. Nesting/content rules are element-specific.
rules.comments: <!-- ... -->; comments cannot be arbitrarily nested and are not a safe container for untrusted text.
rules.variables: No general variables in HTML itself. Template placeholders belong to a separate templating language.
rules.functions: No general function definitions. Event handlers and script elements involve JavaScript or external host behavior.
rules.control_flow: No loops/conditionals in core markup; templates or scripts add them. Navigation/forms have browser-defined behavior.
rules.collections: Elements form a document tree (DOM); lists/tables carry structure but are not ordinary program arrays.
rules.errors: Browsers recover from many parse errors. A displayed page is not proof of valid, accessible or safe markup.
rules.modules: Linked stylesheets, scripts and media are external resources, not language modules equivalent to programming imports.
rules.runtime: Browser/parser produces a DOM and rendering/accessibility trees. Untrusted HTML can trigger scripts, requests or active content when rendered.

languages.example:
Numbers

Total: 6
pitfalls: HTML-to-Python or HTML-to-JavaScript is not a direct language-equivalent port.
Escaping must match text, attribute, URL or script context.
This library displays markup as plain text; it never renders imported HTML.

languages.name: CSS

rules.types: Property values follow property-specific grammars such as lengths, colors and keywords. This is not a general-purpose type system.
rules.blocks: Selectors precede braced declaration blocks; property: value declarations use semicolons. At-rules have their own forms.
rules.comments: /* ... */ only in plain CSS; // comments belong to some preprocessors, not ordinary CSS.
rules.variables: Custom properties use --name and var(--name). They participate in inheritance/cascade; they are not ordinary mutable program variables.
rules.functions: Built-in value functions include calc(), var() and color functions. Preprocessor mixins/functions are separate languages.
rules.control_flow: Selectors, media/support queries and cascade choose applicable declarations; they are not arbitrary imperative loops.
rules.collections: Selectors can match multiple elements; lists of values have property-specific meaning. There are no ordinary program arrays in core CSS.
rules.errors: Invalid declarations are often ignored; unsupported features may fall back silently. Inspect computed styles and browser support.
rules.modules: Stylesheets and @import resources; CSS Modules is a tooling convention. Sass/Less require separate compilation.
rules.runtime: A rendering engine applies cascade, inheritance, layout and painting. Origin, importance, specificity and order influence results.

pitfalls: Specificity alone does not determine the cascade winner.
Browser defaults, viewport, fonts and document structure affect the same stylesheet's output.
CSS is a presentation language; comparing it with code does not create an executable translation.
